name: Alzheimer’s disease death rate
descriptionShort: Annual number of deaths from Alzheimer’s disease per 100,000 people in the United States. This is not adjusted for changes in the population’s age.
descriptionProcessing: We combine NCHS’s historical tables, for 1900 to 1998, with CDC WONDER, from 1999 onward. The historical tables come as one table per period of the International Classification of Diseases, and each names its causes slightly differently, so we match each cause to its name in each table.
datasetName: Causes of death in the United States since 1900
descriptionKey:
- This data comes from CDC WONDER, the mortality database of the US National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), based on death certificates.
- These are crude death rates: deaths divided by the whole population, without adjusting for its age. The US population is much older today than in 1900, so diseases that mostly kill older people, like heart disease, cancer, and stroke, kill a larger share of the population partly because more people live to old age.
- This data starts in 1999. The classification used before then counted far fewer deaths as Alzheimer’s disease, so earlier figures aren’t comparable.

origins.title: Historical mortality tables, 1900–1998 (HIST290 and HIST290A)
origins.description:
These tables from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) give the number of deaths and death rates in the United States for a fixed list of causes, every year from 1900 to 1998, by sex, race, and 10-year age group. Death rates are deaths per 100,000 people in each group.

Before 1933, the figures cover only the “death-registration states”: the states that recorded deaths reliably enough to be included. These grew from ten states and the District of Columbia in 1900 to the whole country in 1933.

Causes of death are classified with the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), which was revised several times over the century. NCHS publishes one table per revision period, and the list of causes grows from 16 in 1900–1939 to 72 in 1979–1998. The names and definitions of some causes change between periods, so a cause’s trend can jump when a new revision comes into use.
origins.citationFull: National Center for Health Statistics. Historical Data, 1900–1998: HIST290, Death rates for selected causes by 10-year age groups, race, and sex: Death registration states, 1900–32, and United States, 1933–98; and HIST290A, Deaths for selected causes by 10-year age groups, race, and sex: Death registration states, 1900–32, and United States, 1933–98. Hyattsville, MD: National Center for Health Statistics.

origins.title: Underlying Cause of Death (CDC WONDER)
origins.description:
CDC WONDER is the online database of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Its “Underlying Cause of Death” data counts every death in the United States, based on death certificates, by the disease or injury that started the chain of events leading to death. The data comes from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which compiles the death records of all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

This snapshot covers the whole country from 1999 onward, for each cause in NCHS’s list of 113 selected causes of death and for all causes together. For each year and cause, it gives the number of deaths, the population, and the crude death rate (deaths per 100,000 people). Causes are classified with the 10th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10).
origins.citationFull: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health Statistics. Underlying Cause of Death 1999–2020 on CDC WONDER Online Database, released in 2021, and Underlying Cause of Death by Single Race 2018–2024 on CDC WONDER Online Database, released in 2026. Data are from the Multiple Cause of Death Files, as compiled from data provided by the 57 vital statistics jurisdictions through the Vital Statistics Cooperative Program.
